extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Plato, classical literature, and political/educational theory
extracted.subtask_description: Close critical commentary on Books III–IV of Plato's Republic, extracting Plato's normative claims about education, art, music, gymnastics, selection of rulers/professionals, and style. Intended to guide interpretation and evaluation of Platonic prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of simplicity (style/subject/metre)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The style is to conform to the subject and the metre to the style; and that the simplicity and harmony of the soul should be reflected in them all.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity is a primary rule to be learned in youth and may be gathered from the creative arts and natural forms; style must fit subject-matter and metre must follow style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of meanness or unseemliness in art
rubrics_metrics.description: “Other artists as well as poets should be warned against meanness or unseemliness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculpture, painting and music must conform to simplicity; those who violate this are to be excluded because they corrupt citizens' tastes and poison souls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music as primary educative influence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of all these influences the greatest is the education given by music, which finds a way into the innermost soul and imparts to it the sense of beauty and of deformity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music affects youth first unconsciously and later becomes allied with reason; therefore musical education must be carefully regulated to shape character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical modes and rhythms must suit moral ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato (via Damon) treats musical measures/ratios and feet (martial, dactylic, trochaic, iambic) as having distinct characteristics that must be matched to style and subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve simple, characteristic melodies appropriate to civic/educational ends; forbid sensuous or corrupting modes (e.g., Lydian/Ionian analogues) that enervate character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastics tailored to role and soul
rubrics_metrics.description: “The soul is related to the body as a cause to an effect ... our warrior athletes must be wide-awake dogs, and must also be inured to all changes of food and climate. Hence they will require a simpler kind of gymnastic, akin to their simple music.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical training should match the guardians' temperaments and civic function: avoid sleepy/indulgent palaestra habits; aim for hardening without brutalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians' diet and simplicity of life
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines drawn from Homer: feed heroes on roast meat only, no fish or boiled meats, no sweet sauces; forbid luxurious cookery and courtesans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple diet and abstention from luxury are part of moral education; excesses lead to medical/legal corruption and degeneration of civic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of private wealth/communal provisioning for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians should have no property; pay only to meet expenses; common meals; not touch gold or silver or be under the same roof with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting property/wealth prevents guardians becoming householders, tradesmen, enemies, or tyrants; private accumulation is an anti-pattern that precipitates ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and testing of rulers (trials by life-events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers must be ‘‘tried by many tests, like gold in the refiner’s fire,’’ passing danger and pleasure at every age victorious and without stain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select those who love their subjects, have passed moral and experiential tests, retained principles under temptation, and show harmonious faculties for the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a civic myth/‘magnificent lie’ as pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Propound a fiction (earthborn men, metals in souls) to rulers, soldiers, and people to promote social unity and devotion to the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myth can be an effective educational device to teach civic duties and justify social arrangements—presented as tradition it fosters cohesion though may be resisted by contemporaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition of ranks / meritocratic mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principles: (1) distinction of ranks dependent on prior circumstances; (2) distinction should be broken through by personal qualities so that rank may change (son of gold may be born of silver, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caste-like divisions should be periodically set aside in favor of merit; construct institutions/tests to enable upward/downward mobility based on fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate experience for professions (physician vs judge)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The physician should have had experience of disease in his own body ... the judge controls mind by mind; and therefore his mind should not be corrupted by crime ... his youth should have been innocent, and he should have acquired insight into evil not by the practice of it, but by the observation of it in others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different offices require different experiential backgrounds: physicians benefit from personal acquaintance with illness; judges require moral innocence and observational knowledge of vice rather than participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of music and gymnastics for soul harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Music tames and refines; gymnastic arouses and sustains—both concern the soul and must be mingled in harmonious concord to produce balanced guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too much music enervates the spirited element; too much gymnastics brutalizes. Education must calibrate both arts to temper disposition and retain courage and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of art: simple, ideal, moral expression
rubrics_metrics.description: “True art is not fanciful and imitative, but simple and ideal,—the expression of the highest moral energy, whether in action or repose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should express moral energy and simplicity, serve as an aspect of reason, pervade nature, and form natural good taste in youth; avoid fanciful imitation that lacks moral ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity/wholeness of a work of art
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of art, like the State, is a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic pieces should achieve organic unity and proportion; parts must fit the whole—this is an organizing principle for both art and polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style must match expressive capacity (avoid disproportion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought should not exceed the power of lucid expression ... there must be proportion between style and subject; no poetry without beauty, or beauty without ease and clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscurity, harsh constructions, distorted collocations, and remote sequences of ideas; ensure language and logic are clear and proportional to the thought expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting archaic obscurity as a model
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurities of early Greek poets arose from their age and are not examples to be followed; the use of language ought in every generation to become clearer and clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern writers should not intentionally return to necessary obscurity of infancy of literature; clarity is a progressive aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about overreliance on poetic authority (Homer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato’s constant appeal to Homer—sometimes altering the text and drawing fanciful inferences—uses Homer as a vehicle of higher truth and as a satirical device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may invoke canonical texts for rhetorical force, but ought to distinguish literal from allegorical uses; such appeals can be persuasive even if original meanings are neglected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve cultural forms to maintain laws and character
rubrics_metrics.description: “Alter the songs of a country, Damon says, and you will soon end by altering its laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protecting established forms of music and gymnastics is crucial because small cultural changes can, over time, alter character, social relations, and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as primary instrument of state health
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is the great matter; without education the state will make no progress; let the guardians take care of education, and education will take care of all other things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize sustained, regulated education (musical, physical, moral) as the foundation for social order and individual self-government rather than relying on minute legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of duty over individual happiness in polity
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution was designed for the good of the whole and not of any one part; ‘first duty, then happiness’ is the natural order of moral ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political arrangements may legitimately subordinate private happiness to collective and moral goods; evaluate systems by their contribution to the state's and citizens' moral ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical practice normative stance (kill or cure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Asclepius and his sons allegedly adopted the ‘kill or cure’ method: citizens of a well-ordered State have no leisure to be ill; remedies which produce sudden catastrophe are sometimes preferred to long coddling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato criticizes excessive medical coddling of intemperate/luxurious individuals and suggests prioritizing public good and robustness over preserving lives made weak by vice; this is a contested normative stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical devices and stylistic tactics to watch for
rubrics_metrics.description: Lesser matters of style: (1) affected ignorance of music; (2) tentative manner in constructing the State; (3) alternating description of the State as reality and imagination; (4) connecting links prepping expulsion of poets; (5) companion pictures and satirical jests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are deliberate stylistic moves by Plato to sustain interest, to satirize, and to prepare readers—useful as rhetorical techniques or analytic markers when evaluating the text's persuasive method.
